turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Most of it made sense. One thing didn't — two buttons at the bottom. Went to the wrong one first. Darker one drew my eye. That wasn't the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The two bottom buttons are stacked with “Continue Shopping” above “Place Order,” making the upper button appear like the main next step in the layout.  
B) The “Place Order” button is positioned below the more visually prominent bottom button, so the intended checkout action feels secondary in the hierarchy.  
C) The bottom button area lacks a clear section label or grouping that distinguishes the shopping-navigation option from the order-completion option.  
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
What specifically in the bottom button area makes “Continue Shopping” look more important than “Place Order” in this layout?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping.' Heavier. More presence. 'Place Order' is the lighter one.

turns.q: If someone saw this checkout screen for the first time, would the lighter “Place Order” button being below the heavier “Continue Shopping” button make the order action harder to locate, or easier to overlook as unavailable?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' pulled the eye every scan. 'Place Order' didn't. Almost went the wrong direction. Re-read both before I moved.

turns.q: If this layout were built exactly as shown, would that re-reading around “Continue Shopping” and “Place Order” be a one-time pause, or a recurring source of hesitation at checkout?
turns.a: Ghost 'Continue Shopping' — no fill, border outline or text link only. Give 'Place Order' a solid fill in a high-contrast color. Visual hierarchy then matches the intended UX: primary CTA reads primary, secondary CTA reads secondary. One CSS property change per button. That's the fix.
